prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening the regime of 10^-18 fractional uncertainty in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part configuration B035 (Katori and Ye) and my citation. The chair asks what physical step makes lattice clocks distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. My answer is that the invention is the magic-wavelength lattice itself: it cancels the light shift on the clock transition so that a very large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held tightly in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel. That trades the single-ion route, limited by quantum projection noise from one particle, for statistical power from many atoms, and it is what made fractional uncertainties at the 10^-18 level and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements reachable. The comb is the counting tool and the ion work is a different platform; neither contains this idea. Ye's group then showed that many-body and collisional effects can be controlled and measured, which is the realization half of an idea-plus-realization pair. The result is reproduced and compared across independent laboratories, no one disputes what was measured, and the credit fits two names. Round 1 sharpened the case for me: seven of eight members converge on it for scientific reasons stated in their own words, including Danielsson, who moved to it after weighing the novelty objection and finding it weaker than he first thought. I do not treat that count as the argument. The argument is that this is the entry on the shortlist where concept, realization, reproduction and consequence are all settled at once. For the citation I keep both the invention and the 10^-18 regime, because the first covers Katori's contribution and the second Ye's, and this wording leaves the Sr and Yb groups' later work as part of a community effort that the prize does not need to claim.
statement.case_against: The reservations are unchanged but I now rate them as manageable rather than decisive. First, overlap with 2005 and 2012: a sceptical member can read lattice clocks as a refinement of an honoured toolkit, and I accept that this is a judgment, not a fact. Second, credit breadth: Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat and the Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST contributed materially to performance and are outside two names, as are ion-clock groups. Third, whether Ye's credit is for lattice clocks specifically or for a wider programme in combs, ultracold matter and many-body spectroscopy; Kroll is right that the citation must keep it tied to the clock. Fourth, the redefinition of the second is pending, so the most visible consequence has not yet arrived. I do not think that waiting for it is required: the prize criterion is a discovery or invention, and the invention and its reproduction are already complete. Fifth, B035 is precision measurement and not the discovery of a new phenomenon, so a colleague who weights conceptual novelty more heavily, as Mehlig and Danielsson do for B008 and B006, can reasonably argue for a second part.

responses.point: Pearce proposes a two-part configuration: B035 with a second part B023 crediting Francis Halzen alone for the conception and leadership of IceCube and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, while acknowledging that Karle and Spiering are left out and that source identification is still at modest significance.
responses.response: I looked at this seriously because the diffuse flux is a real observational window and the Koshiba and Davis precedent from 2002 is fair. But my objection sharpened rather than eased. By Pearce's own account the one-name credit is a compromise: the three-name limit leaves room for only one of the IceCube people beside Katori and Ye, and a collaboration-scale achievement with its leadership reduced to a single name is the kind of attribution I would not want to defend in the citation. Danielsson raises the same difficulty from the other side, calling a three-name selection from a collaboration arbitrary. The science is also less settled than the clock: the origin of most of the flux is unresolved and water-based confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD is incomplete. I do not see that adding a second part improves the prize if its credit cannot be stated cleanly, so I do not add it. If the committee wished to pair B035 with something, I would want the second part to be one whose credit does not need a compromise, and on this shortlist that is a narrower set than Pearce suggests. I leave B023 off my alternatives for the same reason as in round 1, and note that it remains a candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the clearest case of theory, experimental realization and field-wide consequence, but says he would not defend it against a well-argued shift to B035 because of the credit problem; he lists B035 as his first alternative.
responses.response: The chair asks whether three names can handle the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal and the 3D work, and whether the 2016 prize leaves room for the Z2 insulator. On the second point I agree with Eriksson that the 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and Haldane-type phases, so there is room for the time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator. On the first, I do not see a citation within three names that is both honest and short: the HgTe route that Molenkamp measured was proposed by people who are not credited, one of whom has died, and the 3D generalisation by Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan sits outside the set. As a materials physicist I see the ARPES and transport confirmations across many compounds, which is why I keep B008 as my first alternative. But Eriksson's own concession, that B035 is the cleaner proposal on credit, is the point that settles it for me. I did not change my preferred configuration on account of his argument, but it is the one most likely to win me over in a later year if the credit question is resolved, for instance by a citation built on the Z2 invariant and its first observation.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B006 (Higgs) to B035 after reading the opening ballots, finding the overlap objection weaker than he first thought, while still weighing the Higgs discovery higher in pure scientific significance and noting that B035 is more a precision measurement than a new phenomenon.
responses.response: I agree with the mechanism he gives for why the overlap worry is weaker: the magic-wavelength lattice and Lamb-Dicke interrogation of many atoms are a different physical step from either comb counting or single-ion control. I do not agree that a precision measurement is therefore a lesser category. The Nobel criterion says discovery or invention, not only discovery, and I read the committee's task, as I have said publicly, as identifying the topic and the people responsible for the original work, not as ranking the abstract importance of fields. Where I part from him is on the Higgs entry. B006 would need to be framed around two large collaborations with four credited names, and three of them can fit only if we accept a selection that he himself called a proxy-name problem. That is why I keep B035 ahead, though I respect the case that the Higgs is the larger scientific event.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether Ye's credit is for the lattice-clock realization specifically or for a wider programme in combs, ultracold matter and many-body spectroscopy, and whether the citation should centre on the magic-wavelength concept or on the 10^-18 performance, noting also his time in Hall's laboratory in Boulder.
responses.response: His question is the right one and I answer it by tying the citation to the clock. Ye's contribution to this part is the demonstration that the lattice clock can reach the 10^-18 regime and that its many-body and density effects can be controlled and measured; his earlier work on combs and ultracold matter is context, and the citation should not claim it. That is why I keep the phrase on 10^-18 uncertainty beside the invention, so that the wording divides the credit as Katori for the concept and Ye for taking it to the frontier. I also note his disclosure of the Hall laboratory connection. It is a historical tie to the comb environment and not to Katori or Ye personally, and I do not think it requires him to step back from this part, though the committee should record it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom Lamb-Dicke interrogation as a distinct invention rather than as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I regard this as a judgment on which reasonable members differ.
Whether the 10^-18 phrase in the citation adequately conveys Ye's contribution without implying credit for the wider comb and ultracold programme.
How the many Sr and Yb groups, and the ion-clock groups, would view a two-name prize, and whether the citation wording is enough to protect them.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay the prize; I think it need not, but I cannot exclude that others will.

Whether the committee will find a clean attribution for B008 or B023 in a later year; I rely on background knowledge for the exact accuracy records, independent confirmations and the status of source identification in IceCube, not on a verified record.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I am at Chalmers, as is committee member Goran Johansson, whose field of superconducting circuits is the subject of B004 (circuit QED), which I list as my second alternative; I would recuse myself from any deliberation on that part, and I note that I do not rely on it in my preferred configuration. My own field is transmission electron microscopy and I have held leadership in the international federation of microscopy societies, so I may be biased toward B019 (aberration-corrected electron optics), which I ranked first at opening; I do not propose it, and I have discounted it in this round. I note Kroll's disclosure of time in Hall's laboratory and Pearce's Fermi-LAT proximity to B023, and I have weighed them in my responses without asking either to recuse. No personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, or the topological-insulator candidates is apparent from my profile.
